utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dikovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by the Prosecutor will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to your evidence until it's completed. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We were discussing at the end of yesterday what the specific operations of the 37th combat unit was involved in around March 24th of 1999. You directed us to the combat reports that were a part of this operation. The first combat report that we have is P2045 and I'd like to pull that up on e-court. Sir, I'd first like to direct your attention to number 4, in which you indicate what the situation in the territory is and then you go on to say that the unit was carrying out its scheduled activities. You can finish that page. There's page 2 in the English, that again only gives at number 8 main tasks for the day continue with the planned activities in line with the decision to smash and destroy the STS in the Drenica sector. I would ask you what specifically were the planned activities in that sector?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, may I correct you. It's not the 37th combat unit but the 37th Combat Group, and it's a lot smaller. Combat groups are made up of about 250 to 300 men. Now, the activities that we were engaged in on the 27th of March were pursuant to an order from the Commander of the Pristina Corps, as far as I remember, it was Operation Drenica as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What weapons systems were used in that operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this operation, the weapons systems that were used -- well, the weapons of the soldiers were used, automatic rifles which the soldiers were generally armed with. The soldiers had the following weapons: Automatic rifles, the 7.62-millimetre type; the machine-guns, 7.62-millimetres, light machine-guns, that is; then they had the 30.2-millimetres of the self-propelled type; we had 82-millimetre mortars; and we had the 120-millimetre mortars; and we had tanks as well. So that is the basic type of weaponry that we had. Perhaps I've left some weapon out, but I don't think that is essential.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How were artillery targets selected during the operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: Artillery targets were selected on the basis of the deployment and placement of the terrorist forces, and when we saw them in the region, in the area, the locality where the Siptar terrorist forces were located. Now, if they were engaged in firing at the unit, if they were shooting at the unit, then the unit would begin to neutralize them, not only by using artillery weapons. They were well-fortified, trenches and bunkers, which could not be neutralised in any other way but required the use of the system and type of equipment able to deal with these firing points that were so well-fortified and could then neutralize them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How was the fire directed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The artillery fire was directed in the following manner: From the vantage points and observation points, and in front of the artillery pieces in its direct vicinity, in front, behind, to the left or to the right, an observation point is selected where there is a commanding officer who is in charge of the firing, and that observation point is there in order to enable the men to see clearly where the shells are falling in order to correct the fire, adjust the fire, firing. Now, the distance from the firing position - and when I say "firing position," that is when the artillery pieces and the crew are located, and the distance can be up to 2 kilometres away in principle of course - and so from that position you observe where the projectiles are landing and then you can correct and direct the fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were the firing positions in populated or unpopulated areas?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have to be outside populated areas, when I'm referring to artillery firing positions, that's the only way you can function, you can fire from these weapons. And according to the rules and regulations, there is a provision which states that firing positions can be set on large areas, boulevards, squares, large squares, and you can't find that kind of urban location in villages. So the firing positions were always outside the villages for them to be able to function properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So you never ordered any firing positions to be placed in populated areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never ordered any artillery pieces, that is to say howitzers, cannons, should be positioned in built-up areas, in populated areas. Now, in the vicinity of populates areas, to the left, to the right, behind, and in front, yes; but in a populated area itself, no, I never issued orders for the artillery to be positioned there because that was not in keeping with the rules and regulations for the use of that type of artillery support.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: This operation appears to continue on in P2046 from 28 March and it's also given combat report number 1115, which is following 1114. That is the report that you indicated that you expected a large number of civilians at number 3. Why would you expect there to be a large number of civilians in that populated -- or in that area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, it was a populated area. It was not unpopulated. So in that area there were a lot of villages, and around about them many houses which in that area were termed hamlets, a group of houses making a hamlet, that is to say the hamlet not belonging to the actual village but near a village and that's what we term "hamlets." And so there were a lot of villages and hamlets along that axis. Now, why did I report that way, that I said that I expected civilians to appear in the area? When I was speaking yesterday about the way in which the terrorists functioned, I emphasised that very frequently what happened was that they use civilians as a human shield and would let them through the area where combat operations were being -- were evolving because they knew that people were -- that they wouldn't be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you at page 19890 at line 5 you indicated that with regard to -- you had spoken with somebody at the Pristina Corps to discuss what to do in the event you came upon civilians, and somebody from the Pristina Corps was sent to you on the spot in the event that you had to stop operations. Can you please tell me who that person was and how common it was for somebody from the Pristina Corps to come down to answer that type of question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I did send a request asking what we should do, and instead of a response, as far as I remember - and I do underline that, to the best of my recollections - instead of a response through the radio systems communication or written document, an officer arrived from the Pristina Corps. I think that his surname was Okolanski or something like that, I'm not quite sure, but I am sure that his surname ended in s-k-i, ski. Anyway, he arrived and explained to me how I should act. Now, I knew how I should act, I did know, but I waited for confirmation, for confirmation that the knowledge I had was correct; and that was from the command of the Pristina Corps, because I did not wish to make a mistake in my conduct towards the civilians. And, if you're interested, I can tell you what he told me, what this officer told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the officer told me the following, he said that for the movement of the population and care and attention of the population and public law and order generally, that it was the other structures that were in charge of that and that I as a soldier and my unit were not in charge of that --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- That I should stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What were the people -- who were the people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically the police for public law and order and the establishment and the implementation of public law and order, it was the MUP that was responsible, or the police units in other words. Now, in talking to him, we came to the following conclusion: That if any civilians were to appear how we should act, and the conclusion was that we should stop our activities, stop the firing, and send the civilians along a secure axis, in a safe direction, towards a safe area. So that is what I had to do. That was my duty if any civilians should appear. And of course if the civilians needed any assistance, then they should be assisted, and that's something that everybody knows and realizes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to follow-up with that. Did you come across any MUP who actually did assist civilians or did guide them out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not come across any specific example. I can't tell you of a specific example where a MUP member said, Go this way. It was in my area, along my axis, we stopped our firing and took people out. I think in front of me there was some -- or before me there was some MUP members.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: This is in the general area of Izbica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that? I didn't understand the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is this in the general area of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was in the general area of Izbica. I don't know what you mean when you say "the general area," but as far as I remember it was actually in Izbica itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And did you take part of the investigation by the VJ when 101 bodies were found in and near Izbica in graves later on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not conduct any investigation nor am I authorised to do so, to engage in any investigation or investigative activities, no, I'm not authorised to do that and I did not conduct an investigation, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So although your unit was directly involved in that area, no one from the VJ ever called upon you to answer for any of those operations or to provide any information when mass graves were found?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which mass graves you actually mean. At the time that I was there I did not come across any mass graves, no mass graves at all. Let me repeat that. I did not come across any mass graves in that area --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and in the village of Izbica, I did not personally enter that village myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specifically the concern is that the graves weren't there until you already arrived, and it was the activities by the VJ and the MUP in that area that placed those people in the graves; and you were never questioned on that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, please, I can understand this as an accusation against me personally. The army had nothing to do with civilians in that area, no contact at all. Those graves, the graves that you are referring to, did not come into being because of me or members of the army --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so I would like to ask you when you ask your next questions you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... operation. On 29 March 1999 at P2047 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dikovic, could you help me with one matter. We earlier in this case had a witness who were very concerned to make sure we did not confusion operations with actions. You've described this as Operation Drenica. Is it an operation in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I, with my combat group, did not launch an operation at all; that was an action. The combat group, a combat group, does not engage in operations. Operations are something that are done by the army corps and higher units. So this was not Operation Drenica that I engaged in; it was an action to destroy the terrorist forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And before we actually move on to P2047, I have a question. We understand that volunteers began being placed within units sometime around March 24th. Were any volunteers placed with the 37th on or around that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my unit is concerned, there were no volunteers who arrived, or rather, I did not call them volunteers because they were part of the unit, within the composition of the unit, they were in the platoons, companies, and battalions, and they were treated exactly the same as all other members of the unit. So I did not refer to them as volunteers; I called them soldiers. They were probably volunteers because they came forward on a voluntary basis. They wanted to take part in the combat against terrorists, but once they arrived in my unit they were no longer volunteers, they were soldiers, soldiers governed by all the laws, rules --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and regulations that a soldier is governed by.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You indicated before when you arrived on 7 March, you arrived with approximately 200 to 300 individuals. How many volunteers supplemented that number by the time you get to these operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, they were not operations, they were actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, how many volunteers were added to your group after the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period do you have in mind specifically?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On the 24th we have indication that volunteers began pouring into Kosovo. Did that happen in your unit; and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and I think that that's something I said in my report as well, that one man reported to the unit. I think it says "reported." He wasn't sent, he reported, one volunteer; and I think that I stated his first and last name there. Now, what was this about? This volunteer came of his own free will --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he came to the unit alone, himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So on 24 March did any other volunteer report to your unit between the 24th of March and the 2nd of April when the remainder of the 37th arrived?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 24th of March until the 2nd of April, as far as Combat Group 37 is concerned, not a single volunteer turned up; and even if they did, we sent them back.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After the 2nd of April did you receive any volunteers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 2nd of April, I received soldiers. Let me repeat that word, soldiers. I did not receive volunteers nor did I treat them that way, it was soldiers. Soldiers came in an organized fashion and they were deployed in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, page 10, 12, and 13, the witness said that the one volunteer that had shown up, they returned him back, not: "Even if they did, we sent them ..." I mean, it's basically the same meaning. He specifically said about this one volunteer that he mentioned that came, and he said that even that one we sent back and there were no other volunteers in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that what you said, Mr. Dikovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that one volunteer came to us by the 2nd of April and that that one volunteer I sent back from the unit up until the 2nd of April, in the period from the 24th of March to the 2nd of April. One volunteer came himself. He wasn't sent by anyone, he came of his own free will, but I sent him back, this soldier. He wasn't even wearing a uniform; he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you took great pains to say what you would do with a volunteer, that he would be called a soldier, he would be treated as a soldier, that he would have all soldierly duties. You also indicated at page 9, at line 9: "They were probably volunteers because they came forward on a voluntary basis." Who were those people, when did they arrive, and how many were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, perhaps I misunderstood you again. Now, the period from the 24th of March to the 2nd of April, as I said, one single - and I wrote that in my report - one single man reported to the unit and he was sent back from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After the 2nd of April, did any volunteers, or as you call them soldiers, report to your unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I call them by their true name, Ms. Carter. Volunteers did not arrive. It was soldiers who arrived, dressed in military uniforms --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- They looked decent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We can play games with semantics or you can tell me how many members who volunteered to serve in the VJ appeared in your unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise but with your permission I do think the witness should be allowed to answer the question he is asked because in the past few examples Ms. Carter has interrupted the witness in his answer, in the middle of his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, may I be of assistance, Ms. Carter. I'm afraid, Your Honour, that we're moving in two different directions, at cross-purposes, that Ms. Carter is asking one thing and the general is answering something else because the general understood it whether anybody came in civilian clothes as a volunteer, that means this person walking on the street suddenly comes to report, and as far as I understand it, Ms. Carter is asking about volunteers coming to his unit if I've understood you correctly, Ms. Carter, and quite obviously I have so these are two different things -- do you understand me and that's why we're spending so much time about this one man who happened to be passing and came by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, do you have a line reference for the quote that you were giving?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was page 9 at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No -- he said this today?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 9, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If you start running at 4: "As far as my unit is concerned, there were no volunteers who arrived, or rather, I did not call them volunteers because they were of the unit," et cetera, et cetera, "so I treated them as volunteers, I called them soldiers. They were probably volunteers because they came forward in a voluntary basis." That is the group I am interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dikovic, could you concentrate on that group of people and tell Ms. Carter what she wants to know in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was only referring to the period when the 24th of March and the 2nd of April, and that's what the question was about, wasn't it? A single man. After that, soldiers were arriving at the unit, soldiers, in an organized manner. Those people reported on a voluntary basis and they were trained before they came to my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, they're the ones she's interested in. So could you answer the questions she asks you, please, about these people. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: From the 24th of March until the 2nd of April, how many of this group appeared with the 37th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, between the 24th of March and the 2nd of April, as far as my combat group was concerned, there was a single man, no more than one person, who reported who wanted to join the action, and he was turned away from my unit, turned away from the combat group.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dikovic, I'm referring to your own answer now where you said that: "... there were no volunteers ... I did not call them volunteers because they were members of the unit, they were in the platoons ... they were probably volunteers because they came forward on a voluntary basis. They wanted to take part in the combat against terrorists ..." Now, who are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, specifically what I have in mind is Combat Group 37 because the question was about the action, were there any volunteers involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the period, the period, between the 24th of March and the 2nd of April in relation to Combat Group 37 at the time the remaining part of the 37th Brigade was in Raska at a distance of 100 kilometres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dikovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- outside the area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dikovic, do you want to go home today or do you want to come back and finish your evidence tomorrow? You gave this answer: "They were probably volunteers because they came forward on a voluntary basis." Now, I think I understand what you're talking about as confirmed by Mr. Fila. What I want to know is: Your description of who these people were, why were you calling them volunteers, and how many of them were there? Could you deal with that, please, and stop the verbal semantics, as Ms. Carter invited you to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is certainly my intention to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've been asked several times. Please now do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from the day the war began to the day it ended, the day it ended, please allow me to explain briefly about those people. In order to be able to explain this, I have to tell you briefly about what the situation was. So on the 24th of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- combat group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Dikovic, I'm afraid I don't agree with you. Now gave us this answer. Now, you tell us how many people you were referring to when you gave us that description. "They were probably volunteers because they came forward on a voluntary basis." How many of them were in the 37th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the 37th Brigade there were about 100, 150 such people, between 100 and 150 there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now Ms. Carter will continue. She may want to break that down into different groups, I do not know, but she will now focus the questions for you. And please bear in mind we now are clear what we're talking about. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When did these 100 to 150 volunteers arrive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they came while the brigade was still outside Kosovo and Metohija, as far as I remember, outside the area, while it was still in its original area, and that was Raska, the distance from Kosovo and Metohija being about 70 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We've had indication that the triggering event for volunteers to enter these units is at the time war is declared. How were these people coming into your unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, at this time I am in Kosovo. Now, what do I know about how they were coming? That's what I know based on reports coming from my subordinates. They were coming following their training, and the training occurred at Bubanj Potok near Belgrade and in Medja near Nis, this was in an organized manner --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you're saying these 100 to 150 people were attached to the remainder of your brigade that was left at Raska that entered on April 2nd; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now we'll move back to P2047. This document purports to be another combat report of you from the 29th of March, 1999, on the continuation of that operation that we were discussing earlier. Did any tasking or anything change from the last report to this one or did the operation continue status quo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this operation was completed on the 29th, on or about the 29th, completed, this action, action, was completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, there is an amendment to this combat report at P2048; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic. One moment. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. A simple question. If we look at the number and that alone, I don't think the witness has a proper reference point. Perhaps the witness should be handed a hard copy of the document or perhaps we should have it in e-court, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So 2047 was at 11-16; 2048 is 11-16-1, that is an amendment to your original combat report or a supplement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interim combat report, mine, yes, that's right, interim.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At 5.1 it indicates that: "Pursuant to an oral order of the Pristina Corps commander received at around 9.30 hours to take over the assignment and order for further engagement of the unit, the 125th Motorised Brigade commander was contacted and it was agreed with him that the commander of the Combat Group 37 set off to sector 119 and then to Srbica, where only an order was received without any other documents." Can you please tell me, what is the relationship between the 37th and the 125th that's contemplated by this combat report?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time those were adjacent units, neighbouring units, but no more. There was no other special relationship between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When it indicates that it was to take over the assignment and order for the further engagement, did the 37th take in the 125th? Did the 125th take in the 37th? Or does that mean something completely different?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, it's not that a brigade was taking over from another brigade. This is a different thing altogether. If you care, I could perhaps explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Please do, because it's my understanding that the two groups then went on to Srbica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then please explain.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, at this point in time, on the 29th of March, the 125th, or rather, its components are, as far as I remember, in the general Srbica area and they are closer to the Pristina Corps command. It is probable that the commander of the Pristina Corps used a liaison officer from the 125th Motorised Brigade to forward documents to me, and since he was closer to me, since he was closer to me, our liaison officers would join up and my liaison officer would take charge of these documents from the liaison officer of the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, in this specific case we are looking at documents, a simple handover of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And without having to go back to P2047, it indicates at number 8 that it's going to link to -- an order that's going to be started on the next day is 455-90. If you can take my word for it, I would then direct you to P1969, which is that document, 455-90. If you prefer for me to go back, I can, but that is the document it's indicating.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, you mean what I'm looking at on my screen? Is that the document you have in mind that comes up on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, I apologise. P1969, please. And I would hold out to you that this is the order that engaged you once you received -- were received in Srbica starting on March 28th of 1999. Does that seem correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not correct, Ms. Carter. I wasn't involved in this operation, Malisevo. I had received an assignment on the 29th, possibly the 28th, but not about this action in the Malisevo sector. I wasn't involved there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then, unfortunately, we'll go back to P2047 at number 8. As we're bringing it up in English I'll read out to you number 8: "Focuses of the unit for tomorrow. Tomorrow, the unit will act in accordance with order, strictly confidential, number 455-90," which you were just shown, "of 28 March 1999. The task will be completed on 30 March, 1999." Are you telling me that not only was your combat report wrong but P1969 did not engage you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, for the sake of precision can you bring back the order by the Uzice Corps commander so that I can see where the task is in relation to my brigade to see whether it's there, in that order, the previous document; so I can see if there's any reference to my brigade in that document, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just showed me -- yes, yes, a while ago, the one you were showing me a while ago. You showed me the front page, title page of the document that was about the Malisevo document, but you didn't show me what the document was about in the pages after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For ease so we don't have to flip between documents I'll present a hard copy of P1969 to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could the usher please collect that and give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The document on the screen indicates that you are to be engaged at 455-90, and the document you are holding in front of you is number 455-90. Were you given orders under this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Carter, now that I've seen it, yes, item 5.5, paragraph 5.5.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And in 5.5 you have a couple of tasks and it also notes that your command post is going to be in the area of Srbica and it's going to be in a factory. What factory was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a part of a factory -- well, I can't quite put my finger on it now, I can't remember the name, but it was out of operation, and I can't for the life of me remember its name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Was it in a populated area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no, it was outside Srbica. I think this was a facility belonging to the compound of the ammunition factory. That's what I think. I think it was some sort of an ammunition factory, but it was not operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So it was a civilian facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could subsume it under that heading, yes. This was disused facility. It was a factory that wasn't operating and there was certainly no civilians around. Now the factory inside this one single facility inside this entire compound, the factory compound that wasn't operating, no civilians around.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Was the stock cleared out? Was this just an empty building or was it a functioning factory at some point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go into any of the production halls at all or the factory building itself, I didn't go there. I didn't access these buildings, therefore, I can't say if it was empty or not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the operations that began on 28 March 1999.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in those operations, if you mean Malisevo. You see, specifically my role was to reach the Srbica sector, the general Srbica sector, Donje Prekaze and Krusevac to secure the Srbica-Glogovac and Srbica-Klina road and to make sure there was absolute combat control over that territory, and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Excuse me, how did you establish full combat control of the territory?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in this sector that I had been ordered to go to. I deployed my unit there. I set up a security system, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, this operation, it was to end according to P2047 on the 30th of March. Did it, in fact, end at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as far as my unit was concerned. I can't talk about anyone else since there were other units referred to in that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: There are a gap of available documents from the 30th of March until the 19th of April, 1999, when you began operations in Cicavica. Can you please tell me what was your unit doing -- because actually the remainder appeared on April 2nd. What operations were you involved in between the 30th of March and the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 30th of March and 19th of April, the focus was on the implementation of the following tasks. The remaining part, the best part of the 37th Motorised Brigade was received and deployed, and the Drenica sector was occupied. The defence sector was occupied; companies, battalions, and other units did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me when the remainder of your brigade arrived, what was the manpower available?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numerical strength of my unit was about 4.500 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You already had six tanks when you came in with just the smaller group. Did any further tanks or heavy weaponry enter on the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That's right. The entire brigade arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please advise the Court what materials were available to you after the 2nd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had rifles, light machine-guns, machine-guns, mortars, artillery weapons, anti-aircraft weapons, tanks; those were the most substantial weapons that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let's focus on the last three. How many artillery weapons were available to you and what specifically were they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a division, a team artillery pieces and artillery battalion, those were 105-millimetre howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As to the anti-aircraft, how many pieces and what were they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two self-propelled rocket batteries, 30/2; one 20/1 battery; and one battery known as Strela, Strela 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many tanks did you have available to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the brigade a total of 31 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So now you've indicated that until the 19th of April you were deploying and occupying that sector. What was happening? You were just going into your post and sitting there or were operations continuing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, for a unit to enter a sector and take control of a sector, the sector first has to be made safe. Unfortunately, the sectors weren't safe because the terrorists were coming back to the villages yet again, taking up positions, attacking columns, and inflicting losses. At the time, NATO's air force carried out a number of severe strikes on certain targets, and this took some time --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So, sir --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so bit by bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So is it correct to say you were continuing the operations to smash and destroy the terrorist forces in the Drenica region while the remainder of your unit was being deployed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were taking up these positions, our primary task was to defend from any air-strikes, to engage in the fighting with the Siptar terrorist forces, and to take up our defence sector. According to our assessments, the attack would have been carried out by ground forces in addition to air-strikes, obviously. So we gradually entered these sectors and we were engaging the terrorists whenever we came across them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At any time before the 19th were you supporting the MUP in any operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. There must have been joint operations. We probably coordinated our activities. I'm not sure which particular operation you have in mind, but there were some joint operations, as we fought the Siptar terrorist forces, and the MUP forces too took part alongside with us in some of those actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you actually enter an order for defence which is 5D1029, and I would ask for that to be brought up on e-court, which was given an operative number of 125-2. When it comes up on the screen, if you can confirm that it is your document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one thing, can I see the last page, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Since many pages will be --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- just to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Many pages will be referred to, so I think it might be easier to provide a hard copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicate this is going to be a two-phase operation. The first phase was going to last for four to six days, as found at page 2 in both the -- in the English and page 1 in the B/C/S; and the second phase is going to take five to seven days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the enemy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And within this document you provide placement of your individual units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, where they should be in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct you to 5, tasks of the unit, and just briefly confirmed that the 1st Motorised Battalion, and the 2nd motorised battalion, and the 3rd motorised battalion, numbered 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3 all three indicate that they're going to be supported by the 37th artillery group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the man was that the artillery group should lend them support, if necessary, but this didn't necessarily in the case according to this order. It says should the need arise, so this was a plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And as a side note, the 1st Motorised Battalion was going to be placed in a school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This just relates to the command post for the battalion, not the entire battalion, just the command post; that is to say the group that is in command of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So the military was using a school in order to command the 1st Motorised Brigade -- or Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it was empty, the old school, yes; but here it says in the village of S -- the Orlate village. I cannot say whether the battalion commander was in that school or not. I can't remember, but in the area of Orlate village, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now I want to direct you to 5.7 which is on page 6 of the English. This is indicating that the 37th air defence shall protect the 37th Brigade artillery groups for the duration of the tasks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I apologise, but 5.7, you're asking me the question but may I have just a moment to find para 5.7 first before you go on with your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The artillery rocket battalion defends the artillery during the duration of the entire task, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct. What I'd like to direct your attention to is actually the second paragraph of that 5.7, where it indicates that: "During the day and in conditions of good visibility, keep the firing positions in populated areas ..." Sir, I asked you before: Did you ever place firing positions in populated areas, and you indicated not only that you did not but it would be against the rules to do so. Why are you placing firing positions in populated areas under this order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let me just find para 5.7 first and that part of it, paragraph 2. "Firing positions in populated areas, valleys, and in sectors with wooded areas obscured from view and" --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- "good visibility," and so on. Not exclusively in populated areas, Ms. Carter. It says valleys and sectors with wooded areas and obscured from view and air-strikes and only --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Based on your prior answers, firing positions in populated areas should never been option, not even a choice of several. Why were you placing in your orders that you can keep the firing positions in populated areas and who were they populated by?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, they should never be in populated areas for the artillery, I was telling you about the artillery, that's what I was referring to; but here we're dealing with systems for anti-air defence, air defence systems, and a moment ago we were discussing artillery. So this is an artillery battalion for air defence, intended for combat with targets in the air-space; and it can be found in populated areas, only in populated areas where there is no population because they shoot up above, straight up. So we're dealing with the PVO artillery -- artillery battalion. A moment ago we were talking about artilleries, and this is quite a different system.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, even --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery is one thing, this is another.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Even taking in your distinctions, isn't placing firing positions in populated areas when you know that NATO is conducting strikes, don't you believe that that places that populated area in danger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not objecting to the question. I'd just like to stress that the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sit down and let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Carter, we did not set up in populated areas. My units did not take positions in populated areas. There was no population, no people, in the areas, so when I say "unpopulated," what I mean is there are no inhabitants there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, could you now try to bring your cross-examination to an end, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Hopefully very quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Just briefly discussing the Cicavica operations, there's a series of documents that place you in that area 5D1023, 5D1056, P2005, 5D1036, 5D220, and P2591, all of these place you in operations going on through almost May in Cicavica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that's a large number of documents enumerated there. I don't think that the witness can refer to all these documents and have them in his head. He doesn't know the contents of those documents either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You surely can't expect the witness to know what's in documents with particular numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, actually that was direction for both the Court and I'm asking the witness with regards to time that if the Court would choose to look at these documents, that were going to refer to Cicavica operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall of course, but the question for the witness is that he was involved in action in Cicavica into May.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, yes and specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Almost to May.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in the Cicavica action until May. I took part in Cicavica action for a short period of time, and I just took up the blockade line, just the blockade line. I didn't move towards Cicavica. The blockade line had the task of not allowing the terrorists to pull out of the area, so just the blockade line, and it did not go on for such a long period of time, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the -- this answer as well as the length of time that it took trying to suss out the volunteers question, I would ask for more time with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the witness in his examination-in-chief deal with Cicavica and restrict the time that he said he was involved there?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: He certainly gave it a much shorter period than what the Prosecution believes his involvement was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In his examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did he say? Remind me. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Not handy, Your Honour. Mr. Hannis will assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you recollect, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we mentioned Cicavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: He placed Cirez is going to be involved in the Cicavica operation, so another enumerated villages and hamlets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, you can't artificially extend your cross-examination by asking questions you don't need to ask and then getting unsatisfactory answers. If it's not an issue for the Defence, then it doesn't make much sense for you to have asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then I can break down into the discrete issues that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why when there's no challenge to the documents you've referred us to and you could have relied on them but for the fact that you asked that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Again, as to Cirez there was a indication that the involvement with that ended sometime in late March 23rd to the 25th is the time-period I recall. I would like to discuss the operations that were taking place because Cirez is back into play in April, and given what occurred at Cirez as well as the criminal activity that was brushed upon by the Defence when discussing the 37th Motorised Brigade, I need to place them in that area in order to make 5D726 have sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the relationship between Cirez and Cicavica?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specifically at number -- if the Court look to 5D1023, which is a document that I asked to be brought up initially, it indicates at number 4 that the brigade is in Cirez for joint operations. I need to determine when specifically they got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And respect fully, Your Honour, the document P2591 where he describes this entire operation as being like an elephant to kill a fly is also in regards to these Cicavica operations and I'd like to have the ability to explore this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Carter, we made it clear yesterday what arrangement you should try to adhere to. We're not satisfied there's good cause to continue with the cross-examination in this instance, it may be different in other cases. So that is the end of it unless there is something absolutely crucial you would like to ask to complete it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, if I can have a few moments to address 5D726, that's based on the murders that were addressed yesterday and specifically speak to -- unfortunately it's only a B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, it's our Defence document, and it contains the names of people who were prosecuted against whom there was suspicions that they had perpetrated certain crimes. Now, the Prosecutor on Saturday told me that the document wasn't translated; second, that it doesn't have a signature and stamp, and they questioned its authenticity. So we didn't object to that kind of objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that was -- the Court directed a question directly to me with regard to this document when it was stated in court that I had no objection to it. There is a concern of it having no B/C/S translation and receiving it on a weekend when language staff is not available; however, we were fortunate enough in order to have OTP staff that was available, actually another lawyer who provided at least a summary for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following this, I'm sorry. This -- is this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was admitted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is your objection, Mr. Cepic? I'm not -- was it admitted at your instance or at the instance of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this document was admitted, no, it wasn't, Your Honour -- [In English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was marked for identification yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, based on the -- not having an English translation and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but who presented it, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That would be the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, so you've introduced this document yesterday and now you're objecting to the Prosecution cross-examining on it. That can't be right, can it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not questioning that, Your Honour; however, the Prosecutor on Saturday made the objection that the document does not have a signature and stamp, that was their basic objection, and therefore they questioned its authenticity. But I did not object it to be used in the cross-examination or have it admitted, of course. [In English] -- This interruption or confusion. We do not object for admit -- for that document in relation to be admitted, very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So you made a mistake, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please sit down. Please continue, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated you had some brief knowledge in regard to some of the defendants that were noted in 5D726, specifically you indicated you were aware of a man by the name of Stevan Jekic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jekic, yes, Jekic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And if I can provide a hard copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I direct you to page 18 [sic] where it's discussing incident 19. Stevan Jekic was a -- it appears to be a volunteer commander, is that correct; and if so, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 11, I don't seem to have page 11, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have we not already had evidence about Jekic?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The name was mentioned, Your Honour; however, the -- the crimes that are in this document I believe need to be brought to the attention of the Court, especially given the number of them before he was actually removed, because failure to prevent and punish obviously features quite strongly here. The concern is there are multiple crimes by the same person, very vicious and sadistic crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that not obvious from the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the document does not give indication of specific dates of each one of these crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's concentrate on what the document doesn't contain.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Stevan Jekic was a volunteer commander, is that correct, and he joined up with your unit on the 24th of March; is that correct, per that document? Is that a yes? I have to hear you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when Jekic joined my unit, I don't know the exact date, but Jekic was part of my brigade, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, his designation is a volunteer commander. How did you have "volunteer commanders" in your unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was Jekic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jekic was not a commander. He was not the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So that document is incorrect in that aspect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is that Jekic committed serious crimes; it is not correct that he was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, we don't have the English translation right now in front of us but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There isn't one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is not an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it's obvious that there is some confusion because it says "the volunteer Stevan Jekic was" in the Serbian original it says the volunteer, not the volunteer commander that's what I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answers your question. Please continue, Ms. Carter. We cannot allow this continue indefinitely, please bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, there are a number of crimes that are noted by Stevan Jekic, first that he forced a civilian to serve as a human target; second that he killed a mentally retarded man; third that he ordered his men to remove several women from a refugee column, took them to an unknown location, the same column soldiers looted. How long was Stevan Jekic committing his atrocities against these civilians? When was the first incident and when was the last incident when he report was finally filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We haven't got interpretation in B/C/S, Your Honour, it's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No interpretation so you'll need to go through all that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The question is --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask the question, please. There are a number of crimes alleged against Jekic; over what period did he commit them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it's a period -- well, the first half of April, around the first half of April, and all the crimes are listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say "the first half of April," are we discussing a few days? A few weeks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please move to something else. If half a month isn't good enough for you, I'm afraid the time is too late for you to explore it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I will turn you now to incident 20 at page 9 this is a issue of five volunteers committing multiple crimes. They were arresting -- they arrested six men then liquidated them then threw their bodies down the well. Two unknown civilians were liquidated and thrown down a well. One unknown civilian was killed and then buried. During an ordered operation at Gornje Prekaze, 20 civilians were liquidated; four men were taken off a refugee column and liquidated. These five men, how long were they allowed to commit these crimes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I do apologise, but these are five idiots who committed serious crimes, five complete idiots which we managed to capture and prosecute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dikovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and prevent them from carrying on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Answer the question you've been asked. Over what period of time did they commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says between the 10th and 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it actually say that on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the end of your cross-examination, Ms. Carter. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, my colleague of the Prosecution asked you about Izbica, and on the map you explained to us your axis, the direction you moved along. Did you enter the village of Izbica during that critical occasion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, my unit did not enter the village of Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you enter the village of Vocnjak?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit did not enter the village of Vocnjak, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you continue your movements further, as shown in the order, towards the village of Brocna?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stopped the action because civilians appeared in the area, and then I went back. I returned to the area of Srbica. So the action was completed, I went back to the area of Srbica, and took on the rest of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just to go back to the village of Izbica for a moment. Did you ever open fire at the village itself, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the village of Izbica, there was large-scale resistance put up by the terrorists; that is the truth of it. Now, my units, my units I say, did not open fire at the village, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. How long -- how far away from the village were you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stopped my unit at least one kilometre away from Izbica, that's where I stopped, and I did not see it with my own eyes either, not as people have been trying to say that my forces did that. That's just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the Prosecutor mentioned something about schools and said that the soldiers were there. May we have 5D1062 [as interpreted], please, document put up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you take a look at item 4, second paragraph, please, but before you do that just tell me whether this is one of your documents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning -- it's the beginning of June, the 7th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll down, please. [Interpretation] Paragraph 4, please. [In English] Unfortunately it is wrong number. I need 5D1084, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the use of that document; it was not on the original advice list in regards to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that it was on original list, and also this is the question which is from cross-examination, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've been told it's not on the list, so you cannot use the document unless you can demonstrate that it's on a list; and if you can't, then you'll need to ask the question without the reference to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the meantime could we have IC158, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, on our screens we're going to see a map now, and you drew in the positions of the army roughly on that map. Now, would you take a look at the map again, and to the best of your knowledge could you draw in the positions of the terrorist forces, if you can remember where they were.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, can we zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... In the blue colour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm a little nervous now, to be honest, because you're all watching the general draw and drawing was never my strong point. Mr. Cepic, this is along the axis of my unit. As to the other units, do you want me to draw in that because I don't really know?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, General, that will do. Just your line.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have an IC number, IC159, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the document to appear on our screens, General, in your combat reports did you perhaps report that you did not have any units deployed in school facilities after the 15th of May, or rather, mid-May 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic, I did receive an order from the corps commander, and as of that date, as I reported on this, that we did not have any forces in any school buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please use this other map, and you know what I'm talking about, my learned friend from the OTP asked you to draw something yesterday, so the same question in relation to your unit but the deployment of the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do the blue lines on this map represent?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's not been translated. What do the blue lines represent?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the lines that were reached, as far as I remember, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the last portion of counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lines reached, the lines that I eventually reached, in that action. That is what I marked in blue yesterday. That's what the OTP asked me to do, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're now being asked to mark where the terrorists were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, just for the sake of the record, can you tell us what these lines that you've just drawn mean and what about the blue circles you just drew there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The two blue lines were there before, Mr. Cepic, and they were the point that he reached; and the circles are now where the terrorist forces were deployed, as you asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this can have an IC number, can it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you one more time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I think it's time for our break and time for the end of your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, just one question with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, my final opinion [as interpreted]: What was your opinion of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that did not arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you cannot ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dikovic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours. It was an honour for me to present my point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just one thing. My learned friend from the OTP and I agreed. I have two exhibits to tender, 5D1026 and 5D1087.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're presenting these by agreement or -- are these documents that are not already yet exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, they're not exhibited. We didn't actually use them during our chief, and they had been announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're both agreed that the Trial Chamber should consider the contents of these in their deliberations?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, all we are agreeing is that there is no question about their authenticity, and we would assume that they're going to be brought in here either through a bar table motion, and so for ease of the Court we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's unsatisfactory to start chopping and changing the arrangements. When you make your next motion for admission of documents from the bar table, assuming these are not spoken to by any other witness, then these should be included in your motion because that will focus for us the matters to which they relate and give the OTP the opportunity of responding if they think it's appropriate. So we will deny them admission at this stage. We shall resume at ten past -- in fact, we'll resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Return to Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to use this opportunity as we're waiting for the witness. Last Friday I still had to give you the number of that video clip that we showed on Friday, the 7th of December, to witness Stojanovic. Just for the sake of the record, if I may say, this is 5D1378, so that's the number that I still owe you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Stamp will continue in a moment. Please remember that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of the evidence continues to apply throughout your evidence. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. When we left off last --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- we were speaking about what witness K-83 had to say about the involvement of his military police unit in certain crimes at Meja. We've also had evidence before the Court from a former member of the technical company of the logistics battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade that during an operation at Ljubizda Has in December 1998 his unit was ordered along with the military police to expel people from that village, and the military police in fact were involved in expulsions of people from that village at that time. Were you, as a commander of the military police in the Pristina Corps, aware of the operation in Ljubizda Has in December 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never said that I was the commander of the military police. The military police, if it's the 52nd Battalion of the military police you have in mind, had their own commander, it was Major Stevo Kopanja. In terms of command, the military police battalion was always subordinated to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we have your evidence about that. Please deal with the specific point here, about whether you personally knew of the operation at Ljubizda Has.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I personally did not know about that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you at any time become aware of any investigations into the conduct of the military police in those operations after the operation was completed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. There are a couple other things I would like to clarify. Last time you were here you said that you were not aware of any drastic problems in respect to the cooperation between the forces of the Ministry of the Interior and the VJ, apart from a dispute that arose at Glogovac in respect to a mopping-up operation there and --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there were no problems in terms of the cooperation between members of the military security service, members of the MUP, and members of the State Security Service in terms of exchanging information and carrying out activities. That's what I said the last time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Visnjic whether or not you or any group associated with the Pristina Corps had reported that the MUP members were committing crimes on the ground, serious crimes, against the civilian population and attributing them to units of the VJ; and you said you did not make any such reports. Do you recall that question and your answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there were some problems in terms of the cooperation between members of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes --
