utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and commanders of units on the ground. It was in that context that I referred to the problem of cooperation in the area of Drenica, or rather, Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You're returning to the question I asked before that. May I just read to you the question Mr. Visnjic asked you and your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While I try to find it. Are you aware that General Pavkovic had reported to General Vasiljevic and General Ojdanic that there were some 800 bodies, that is, cadavers, that is, deceased persons that the MUP was making claims of against the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that information. The information that I'm aware of is this: The commander of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic, informed the army command about cases of poor cooperation between army units on the one hand and MUP units on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that General Pavkovic said during the conflict that the MUP was blaming the VJ in respect to 800 -- the bodies of 800 deceased persons? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I do know is this: The corps commander, General Lazarevic, complained about the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. Please stop. You've answered the question. You've said: "No," you've answered it twice. Let's move on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic told us in evidence that you told him about the people or about two people who gave information over to the office -- to the army regarding the number of 800 bodies alleged to be found in Kosovo. Do you recall telling General Vasiljevic about 800 bodies alleged to be found in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that to General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the General to answer the question, but one thing that I'd like is for Mr. Stamp to provide a reference for Vasiljevic allegedly saying this, having heard from General Stojanovic about these 800 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that's at page 8760 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In -- while we're finding this, in any context did you know about any investigations in respect to 800 bodies of deceased persons in Kosovo during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which case, General, it would be redundant to ask you about any inquiries or investigations that you conducted in that regard. You conducted no investigations in regard to this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the military security service were conducting investigations in relation to each and every case where they were indications that certain crimes had been committed by members of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking about 800 bodies for a specific reason because this is what -- this is the evidence we have and -- just a minute. What we have here is General Vasiljevic being asked this question: "Do you know where this number, 800, came from," that's 800 bodies, "who had come up with that number and how." And he said: "I don't know how they came up with that particular figure, but we have two persons according to what Colonel Stojanovic had told me handed that information over to the army," and this is at page 8760 of the transcript. Anyway, you have already said you know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Visnjic: "General, did you ever report - and when I say 'you,' I mean your organ or the corps command - the following: Acting independently on the ground a number of members of the MUP and entire small units are perpetrating grievous crimes within the Siptar civilian population within the villages or refugee camps, murders, rapes, looting, aggravated theft, and so on, and they are deliberately ascribing these crimes or appearing to ascribe them to units or individuals of the Army of Yugoslavia?" And your answer was: "I never said anything to this effect." What I'd like to ask you is this, go back to the question that Mr. Visnjic asked: Did any of your organs or any organ of the corps command, and not necessarily you personally, make that report?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my answer to you is this: There are problems. I'll give you a direct answer to your question, that there were problems in the area of Drenica and that the command of the 37th Motorised Brigade on several occasions stated that when his units arrived to these localities they came across individual or -- individual bodies or groups of bodies, and then the corps command through the military police of the investigating organs, the security organs, they took on complete investigations, and that's what I reported to the corps command about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Listen, I just repeated precisely the question that Mr. Visnjic asked you. Mr. Visnjic asked you the question and he asked you if any organ of your security service, not necessarily you personally, made that report; and your answer was that: I did not make that report. What I want to ask you is: Separate and apart from yourself, did any organ of your security service make a report that the MUP were committing serious crimes against the Siptar civilian population and ascribing those crimes to the VJ? Did -- was that report made?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not, but the subordinate organs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Might I be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You've answered the question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you refer to the command of the 37th Motorised Brigade, are you referring to Mr. Dikovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have had in evidence a report from the army commander, General Pavkovic, and this is Exhibit P1459, in which he says -- and I'll just read from the document I have. "I has been established beyond doubt and we have already reported on it in regular and combat reports that due to noncompliance with the resubordination order some MUP members and to a considerable extent smaller units which operate independently on the ground are committing seriously crimes on Siptar civilian population in settlements on refugee shelters, murder, rape, plunder, robbery aggravated theft, et cetera; and they purposely attribute or plan to attribute these crimes to units and individuals in the VJ." This is precisely the same thing that Mr. Visnjic asked you about. My question is this: Do you know which reports General Pavkovic would have gotten this from? Who reported this to General Pavkovic if not your security service?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and explain this to you again because quite obviously you don't understand me. We had in several locations, not to repeat them now, in the general Drenica area, and in three locations in the Lipljan municipality area, we had a situation in which the units when coming to the locality would either come across individual bodies or groups of bodies or the authorities of the Ministry of the Interior would inform unit commanders of the corpses. And we clarified all these situations operatively. Now, I don't know what Mr. Pavkovic had in mind, probably it was these situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these civilian bodies you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the entire team of pathologists and investigating judges and crime workers established that there were civilian bodies in addition to the KLA bodies, at least that was what the reports of the teams that spent time on the site said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's the same situation as Dikovic spoke to you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, except that over there, there was another unit, I mean in the area of responsibility of that other unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With respect to these bodies that you are talking about, was -- or were the deaths of these persons being ascribed, that is, the civilians, being ascribed by the MUP to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was MUP, but I do know that both commanders complained that there was the possibility that members of the MUP ascribed this to the army and that they reported to their commanders that on these localities the army did not perform combat activities or was not in those locations at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to another topic. Just a couple questions about this meeting on the 1st of June -- or early June, as you put it, 1999, at the Grand Hotel. Before you spoke to General Pavkovic on the phone, did you know of the plans to have a meeting at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Up until that time, did you know of the topics or topic of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that General Lazarevic and General Pavkovic were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know. I was invited by General Lazarevic to attend the meeting, and I informed him that I had a team from the security administration of the Supreme Command led by General Vasiljevic; and then he said that General Vasiljevic should come too, should go to the meeting with me -- I'm sorry, General Pavkovic I meant to say, not General Lazarevic. I don't know what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I think you made a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But whether it is a mistake or not, can I just say, please, if such things arise it should not be corrected from counsel's row.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we'll deal with the propriety of any corrections that counsel seek to draw to our attention, and it's open to you to make any submission you wish in that context. It's not for you to run the court, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sorry if that was the appearance. Sometimes things are said aloud inadvertently and the Court might not hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different matter. That's not what I thought you were referring to. You're talking about stage whispers, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I think it was inadvertently, but it did correct the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Well, I agree with that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So why -- well, you just said you are not aware that General Lazarevic or General Pavkovic would be there. I thought you said earlier that - and that is the last time you were here - that because of the increased security conditions of wartime you would be aware through the security service of the attendance of General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic at meetings. Is that still your evidence or do you wish to change that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I once again state that I was not aware of any such meeting, I was not invited to any such meeting, and I didn't know what that meeting was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a slight side issue. You just said, you just said, that you did not know that General Pavkovic would be attending a meeting in -- that day at that place, you did not know that General Lazarevic would be attending the meeting. Now, I recall that in an answer to a question from the Bench you said that you would be aware of their attendance at meetings in 1999 because of the added security, that is, the security services would have to provide, during the war. Is that still your evidence, that you would be aware of their attendance at meetings in 1999 or do you change that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with your observation. First of all, when I said that as chief of the security organ I would have been informed that meetings were taking place, then the question was whether I was aware and knew about meetings being held of some sort of Joint Command. And I said on that occasion that in that sense, in the sense of providing security for the place and the commander, I would have responsibilities. Now, the second part of your question, of course I knew that at this meeting that you're asking me about now, that General Pavkovic would be attending because he invited me to attend that particular meeting; but I did not know whether General Lazarevic would be present and whether anybody else would be present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from yourself and General Lazarevic, who else was present, if anybody, from the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 3rd Army, except for the commander of the army, General Pavkovic, nobody else was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you send reports to this body that you heard of being referred to as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you heard from General Djakovic, I think, about this body called the Joint Command. Did you at any time send reports to this body that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard from General Pavkovic of the term "Joint Command" for the first time and that -- well, Colonel Djakovic, he wasn't a General, Colonel Djakovic told me there were meetings of coordination and cooperation and mutual information between representatives of the corps and members of the MUP in Kosovo, and let me answer your question. May I finish? And I said that I kept a regular log-book or work book with all the information, and it referred to the activities, the location, the strength of forces, and the overall security situation in Kosovo and Metohija that the security service had. And we sent this to Colonel Djakovic and later on Colonel Radojko Stefanovic, who replaced Colonel Djakovic; and he in turn informed, I assume, the competent MUP authorities and the State Security Service about that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question again. Do you remember the question I asked you, General, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I sent any reports to this so-called Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not send any. I just made my assessments and gave them to the head of the operative department, who then informed the Joint Command of those appraisals and assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did your security service receive any reports from this so-called - to use your phrase - Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the meetings that you call the Joint Command, when I would come back from the chief of the operations department, I would go down to see him and I would receive from him information and data which the MUP organs had at their disposal, as did the security services, with respect to the topical security situation in Kosovo and Metohija, first and foremost with respect to the terrorist activity there and the open roads, the communication lines, kidnappings, attacks against certain Serb enclaves in Kosovo, and that information, in addition to my own knowledge, I regularly incorporated that into my reports sent up to the superior organ of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again - and I'm not saying that you are being evasive, you just haven't answered my question - Joint Command, this is an expression that you have used, did you or your organs of security receive reports from the so-called Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive reports. I received notes setting out information which the MUP of the SDB, the SDB organs in their exchange of information presented their knowledge on terrorist activities. So if you mean written reports, no, I did not receive those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you about the MUP, I'm not asking you about civilian defence, I'm not asking you about the government; I'm asking you about this body that General Djakovic referred to as the Joint Command. And I ask you again, I'm not asking about you personally either, did members or any part of your security service receive reports from the so-called Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not receive reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were the forward command posts of the Pristina Corps located or -- sorry, withdrawn. When was the forward command post located of the Kosovo Heroes Barracks in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post of the barracks Kosovski Junaci from Pristina, I have no information of that kind. The commanders of my security organ might, but at a number of locations outside the barracks because the barracks were never -- the barracks were emptied and evacuated with the bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think the interpretation was correct, so let's not make a mistake. I don't want to put words into the witness's mouth, but could Mr. Stamp ask the question again because the interpretation of that question was different in our -- the one we got and I think has created some confusion. So could Mr. Stamp ask his question again so that he can be interpreted again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, could you do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the forward command post of the Pristina Corps located at the Kosovo Heroes Barracks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post of the Pristina Corps was never located in the Kosovo Heroes barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said that -- I mean, if you said that, that would be a mistake then, wouldn't it -- or never mind, withdrawn. Could we have a look at 3D1004. Do you know who Slobodan Djindjic was or is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was Colonel Slobodan Djindjic, the deputy chief of the security department of the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did -- was he at any time subordinated or resubordinated to the Pristina Corps during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, during the war in the security sector of the Pristina Corps, very often the assistant chiefs of security or the security department of the 3rd Army command were frequently there, and amongst them Colonel Slobodan Djindjic mostly. Now, he wasn't subordinated to me; he could only be my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do we have 3D1004? That document at the top left, it indicates it's from the Pristina Corps command, security section, strictly confidential, dated the 21st of August, 1998. Could we scroll to the last page, the last part of this document where there is the signature. Oh, there is none on -- well, it's not signed but are you familiar with this report? Is this a report that emanated from your section?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no signature because it's a telegram. I assume it has a rectangular stamp because it was encrypted. I am familiar with this document, and Colonel Slobodan Djindjic is in the corps. Because if somebody from the security department of the 3rd Army would spend time in the security sector of the Pristina Corps, then as the most senior he would sign telegrams sent by the security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at page 1 of the B/C/S, which is page 2 of the English version, and at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read paragraph 3 there, the first sentence at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the operative report of the Joint Command for KiM, we would like to mention the following information submitted by the State Security Service, the SDB."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you will see it goes on to give three bits of information received from the Joint Command of KiM.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- states on its face that your security section received reports from the Joint Command of Kosovo and Metohija. It is -- is it still your evidence that organs of the security section did not receive reports from any so-called Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still claim and state that the security organs of the Pristina Corps did not receive any written reports from, as you call it, that coordination as you call it, the Joint Command. Now, with your permission I'd like to explain what you've just shown us on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if a document has been shown to the witness, or rather, mentioned to the witness, then I think the witness should be allowed to explain what it says there, if a document is put to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As Mr. Stamp has invited him to do. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] High-ranking officers, I said a moment ago, are the military security service from the security department of the 3rd Army frequently went to visit the Pristina Corps command; and on that occasion they went to the forward command post of the 3rd Army, they also went to the MUP organs, the State Security Service, and they would go down to see the chief of the operations department to be informed of the information and data that that department had from the meetings of coordination and exchange of opinion and information. And here Mr. Djindjic states what information he received from the chief of the operative department of the Pristina Corps upon returning from those meetings of coordination and collaboration which took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid that baffles me. Why does he say: "From the operative report of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija"? Why are these words there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really don't know. He probably means operative information and not operative reports that the Joint Command has, or rather, that organs of the MUP and the state security have. That is always what the reference is about, but he personally put together this telegram so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand the notion that you try to convey to us, that it's the Pristina Corps command that actually does the commanding, but here we're talking about a report. So why would a report be by a Joint Command that doesn't exist? Can you help us understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid that in this case Mr. Djindjic is entirely unfamiliar with the term, or rather, with the function that these coordination meetings between the MUP and the army had, and I think in a purely terminological sense he entirely misses the mark here. I have no other remark to make. We received no reports, the security organs of the Pristina Corps received no reports from the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he has not only misunderstood Joint Command, but he's also invented the idea of an operative report by the Joint Command? Is that what you're saying? I want to understand just how far this goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have an interpretation problem. Could the question be interpreted again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I will give you the question again. Are you saying that Djindjic not only misunderstood the idea of the Joint Command but also invented, made up, the idea of an operative report by the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djindjic here shows information that he received from the head of the operative section of the Pristina Corps command, but I think this is phrased in a very unfortunate way. I have no other comment. There is no operative report by the Joint Command that actually reached the security sector of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us that you were familiar with this document. At the time this document was sent, did you see that reference to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, let me inform you of the following: Frequently, not so rarely - or to be more accurate - there were situations when I was on the ground when the most senior officer in this security sector of the 3rd Army, representative of the 3rd Army, put together these telegrams. I didn't say that I saw him at the very moment he was typing it, sending it, but I'm familiar with the general format of these telegrams, I'm familiar with documents like that. But at the moment of the actual sending, I was not familiar with the substance of the document because I must have been aware somewhere on a mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You said that you were familiar with this document that I showed you, that is why I asked you the question; but I take it that your answer now is that you were away and you are not familiar with that particular document. Very well. Do you recall giving an interview to the press sometime in 2002, in which you discussed the events that occurred in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have P2945 brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall giving an interview?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke several times and gave interviews to press agencies in my country. If you let me have a look, perhaps I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is 2945 up? Perhaps I have the wrong number -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's you there in uniform, General?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You remember this interview that this news report refers to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an interview that I gave to Nedeljni Telegraf, the Sunday telegraph. You asked me a while ago whether that was in 2000, I can't actually see if it was in 2002, actually I think it was in 2002, if you could let me have a look at the date, perhaps I can tell you. I can confirm that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the date --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So -- and your picture is there with a caption --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- which says: "For everything, there are proofs and thousands of reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at page 2 of this document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are these reports that you supplied in the course of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could expand the one or expand the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need. These are documents that I gave the journalist of this magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And they are documents that were regularly issued from the security section of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are not documents that were regularly issued from the security section of the Pristina Corps. On the left-hand side is a document that occasionally, or rather, this is information that was submitted to the republican state security centre in Pristina. This was a regular exchange and this is the same kind that I received from the State Security Service. The other document is about my knowledge about the location of the activities and the plans of the Siptar terrorists, and it says: "To the Joint Command for KiM," Kosovo and Metohija. If you want, I can elucidate on both.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let us talk about the second one. The second one is one --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, there is a translation of the second one at page 10 -- could we find -- page 10 of the English in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stamped and signed document dated the 11th of November, 1998, addressed in bold to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, signed with the stamp by yourself, in which you report on a variety of matters arising from operative intelligence. Before we begin to explain, is it still your evidence that you never sent reports to any organ, so-called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you asked me whether I meaning as some sort of a regular practice or form reports to any Joint Command, and I said no --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I did not. I asked you three or four times before you answered the question whether or not you sent reports to the so-called Joint Command, and finally after the fourth attempt I think you answered unequivocally: No. Do you wish to change that answer? Did you in fact send reports to a body described as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer that question if you allow me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But -- yes, and I'll allow you to --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you did send reports to a body described as the Joint Command --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp is saying: Yes, yes, I will allow that, and then he's insinuating: So you did. Can he please first wait for the answer to be given and then he can ask the new question because the question hasn't been answered yet and yet we have a new question already, so the witness is confused. He doesn't know which one he's supposed to be answering, does he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you have been asked, Mr. Stojanovic is: Did you, in fact, send reports to a body described as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I sent no reports at all to any body allegedly called the Joint Command. The document that is now in front of me, and there must be less than a dozen other documents like that, were documents that I submitted to the head of the operative affairs sector upon orders by General Pavkovic whenever he spoke at briefings, the collegium briefings, on the activities by the Siptar terrorists. Once I was out of the collegium I asked Colonel Djakovic, saying that we should inform both the MUP and the state security, and then as soon as we would get up out of one of these meetings I said well: What format? And he said, Well just type up what you know. How should I type it up? And he said, Just put Joint Command there and I'll present this on your behalf including whatever information the military service happened to be in possession of. Mr. Prosecutor asked me whether I ever sent or in a permanent form any reports to the so-called some sort of Joint Command, and my definite answer is: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you attend collegium briefings with General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that he was corps commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said something about less than a dozen documents are the documents like this. How many reports or documents of this nature did you sign and stamp with a seal of your organ? How many?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the figure that I mentioned, ten, is far too big, it's less than that, very few documents, and they should be in the military security service archives and the same thing applies to all these other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say about ten.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far less than ten, a handful. I can't say. You're asking me to say but I can't say. It's certainly far less than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When, can you recall, was the last one that you sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness never said he sent that. He even explained that he gave it to Djakovic. Again the Prosecutor is asking him: When did you send, and forth. I don't know whether using every single question my learned friend Mr. Stamp, why is he trying to trap this witness with each and every one of his questions. I don't think that's being fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If he handed it to General -- well, he handed one to General Djakovic, it certainly could be termed that he sent it, but just to avoid unnecessary argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the last document of this nature that you signed, that you prepared and signed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when the last one was, but I think it was sometime in late October, certainly by mid-November, that's how long I had been providing such information to General Pavkovic; and after that, to the extent I can remember, there was no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this one is dated the 11th of November, 1998. If this was not the last one, how long after this one was the last one sent?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I can remember, didn't I? But I'm sure that as of mid-November I never forwarded any such information again, and I went far less often to Colonel Djakovic in order to exchange information with him, to seek information that the MUP or the State Security Service had in their possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I see the end of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that is the next page, page 11 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is there any indication on this document that it was being copied to either the state security or the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is nowhere to be seen in this document, but I did explain a while ago that when Colonel Djakovic and I came out of General Pavkovic's room, he told me that I should write up this information. What title should I put, what addressee? And he said, Put Joint Command. I wrote it up and I handed it over to Colonel Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just the one copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, not just the one copy. There are rather -- yeah, just one copy of this kind because we processed this sort of information in our telegrams, otherwise, as you can see, this information is in relation to. I'm not sure if there is a translation of this, what I said about the activities of the Albanian terrorists and political players in Kosovo and Metohija. This information had been processed through the telegrams that the corps would send every day to the security sector, the army security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The information -- and you're familiar with the document. Information in this document is comprised of various bits and pieces of intelligence reports about various activities that were occurring in Kosovo. Is it your evidence that you were getting, you as a chief of security, was getting this information from your corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not the sort of information that I received from the corps commander. It was me who informed the corps commander of any information that the service by using proper methodology, the prescribed methodology, had obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. How often did General Pavkovic attend meetings of this so-called Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know how often General Pavkovic attended meetings, these meetings that you refer to as meetings of the Joint Command. But I was well familiar with the methodology of the command's work, and this is what it comprised. If I may, I will answer your question, but you need to allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have. You said you weren't aware of how many meetings of the so-called Joint Command he attended; that's all I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I would like to hear the rest of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- answer, even if you don't want to hear it, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, during the war in Kosovo and Metohija, the situation was a very dynamic one. It was normal for the command to meet in small groups, and then there would be briefings by organs of the command. It was often my responsibility to track down the corps commander. We're talking about 1998 now. So those meetings were regular, daily. When a meeting was over, normally about 1800 hours, the corps commander would then get the specific proposals on how to use certain units and reports on problems that a unit was encountering. He would go to the forward command post of the 3rd Army and tell them there about what had been done, and he would propose a decision to be taken. And then after that, based on what information I had, he would go and meet the MUP organs in order to have coordination for this decision that had been obtained, and then this was verified by the 3rd Army forward command post. At these meetings, as far as I know, in addition to members of the MUP and the corps commander, there were also quite often - I'm telling you something that is second-hand knowledge now because I was never there myself - also people from the State Security Service who also shared their information, information which they had, which made it possible for me to adjust my own assessments or perhaps allow them to adjust their own assessments about the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I -- I'm sorry. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said when Colonel Djakovic told you about the Joint Command, he did not tell you where those meetings took place but you were able to learn this from persons who worked in the security detail for the corps commander and you told us where those meetings were held. Did you learn from these persons who reported to you about these Joint Command meetings we are speaking of how often General Lazarevic attended those meetings, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, based on what I know, General Lazarevic spent virtually most of his time at the corps forward command post in the Djakovica garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So do you --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether and how many times he attended those meetings that you term the Joint Command meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let us know when it's convenient to break, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could take the break now, Your Honours. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Stojanovic, we have to break for half an hour, so could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said just before the break: "I'm telling you something that is second-hand knowledge now because I was never there myself. Also people from the State Security Service who also shared their information, information which they had, which made it possible for me to adjust my own assessments or allow them to adjust their own assessments about the situation in Kosovo." You're speaking about these meetings, these Joint Command meetings, that I was asking you about. How did you get information about or from the State Security Service that was discussed in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1998, I had regular contacts with the chief figures in the State Security Service, and we exchanged information, as provided by the rules, written information or oral information, through personal contact. But since the NATO aggression, this scope of information exchange was greatly reduced because the general security situation was quite exceptional, so very often I wasn't able to find their locations, nor were they able to find me because I was touring units and in the units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was just referring to your answer in answer to questions about these Joint Command meetings you said also present were State Security Service people who shared their information at these meetings. Who informed you about the information shared by the state security at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the operative department of the Pristina Corps command, General Djakovic, put to that me and then Radojko Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who is Radojko Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Radojko Stefanovic was from the beginning of 1999 -- well, he replaced Colonel Djakovic as chief of the department for operative affairs of the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think -- well, I don't have the exact information, but as far as I remember it was as of January, the month of January 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So he -- well, you also said earlier, and I think I should put this to you before I ask you the next question, that the information that the transmitted to you from the State Security Service or from what the State Security Service shared with you at these meetings made it "possible for me to adjust my own assessments or allow them to adjust their own assessments about the situation in Kosovo." Now, I take it from that that you were also transmitting to the State Security Service at these meetings information about the situation in Kosovo. Through whom did you transmit your information, the same people, Colonel Djakovic and Stojanovic -- sorry, and Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think that you intentionally or unintentionally are not understanding my answers in the way I gave them, so let me repeat. During 1998 at a time when there wasn't a war on and when the situation wasn't as complex in Kosovo and Metohija, I, through -- exchanged information with the State Security Service, usually personally, through my personal contacts, that is to say I would go to see them, or through written information, which I sent to them or they sent to me. Now, during the NATO aggression there were just a couple of contacts of this kind because the overall security situation was such that, quite simply, we were not able to meet or to share and exchange information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You keep, sir, reverting to various meetings you had with these people, and I keep telling you, I am only asking you about these meetings described to you by General Djakovic as Joint Command meetings. I'm not asking you about any other meeting. And in answer to my questions about these meetings you said that you shared information or transmitted information to the State Security Service which allowed them to adjust their own assessments about the situation in Kosovo, and this was at these meetings that I'm asking you about. Did you transmit to the participants of these meetings any information about the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, when some important information for the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija, I would inform, in addition to the commander and pursuant to the commander sometimes from time to time the chief of the department for operative affairs, who I assume most probably sent that information on to the State Security Services. And according to my information they would sometimes attend those plans, meetings, and coordination meetings in the MUP in Pristina. Now, when the chief of the operative department came back from these meetings, he conveyed to me the state security's assessments and appraisals of the situation, and on the basis of everything I knew I would correct my opinions and knowledge or confirm what I knew about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija using that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As part of your responsibilities as chief of the security sector for the Pristina Corps, did you report up to General -- sorry, to the chief of the security section in Belgrade, that is, General Dimitrijevic and later on General Farkas, the activities of your commanders, that is, your commander, General Lazarevic and General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules and regulations regulating the work of the security organs of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I was not duty-bound to inform the chief of the security department about what the corps commander and army commander was doing, but I was duty-bound to inform him about all questions from the remit of the military security service, and within that framework about all the activities of the units and the security implications given those activities. Now, during 1998, on a regular basis, pursuant to orders from the security department of the General Staff of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I sent telegrams out with all the things I noticed about security and the security administration General Staff of Yugoslavia and the security section of the 3rd Army. And when the NATO aggression started, pursuant to an order from the chief of security of the 3rd Army, I just sent him telegrams and reports about all matters that the Pristina Corps security organs were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many, if any, civilians attended these meetings that were described as Joint Command meetings to you by Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by Colonel Djakovic that most often those meetings were attended by representatives of the staff of MUP for Kosovo and Metohija and also by individual representatives from the State Security Service and from time to time that Mr. Sainovic attended and various other politicians who happened to come by to be better informed about the overall security situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you informed that Mr. Minic and Mr. Andjelkovic also attended these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information on several occasions that during his stay in Kosovo and Metohija, Mr. Minic did attend. As to Mr. Andjelkovic, he was the president of the Executive Council of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, and I don't have any knowledge about him attending those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As chief of security for the Pristina Corps, wasn't it your duty to discover who attended these meetings that you were transmitting military secrets to? Because you indicated to us that you were transmitting information to them about what was happening in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I informed the competent authorities in the command, and where my commander was present, where my commander attended, I do not -- I had no reason to doubt who this information would be presented to because the commander was duty-bound to be informed of all information of a security character in the corps. So I don't know to what extent and how, but I assume that Colonel Djakovic, from information I provided, would inform the public security organs about certain issues. And finally, we were in charge of the overall security situation together. We had the same enemy, and that was Albanian terrorism. So it would seem logical, would it not, that we exchange and share information when it comes to discussing the same problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You can't tell us precisely about the civilians in attendance at that meeting. General Vasiljevic said that you told him that you were reporting to General Dimitrijevic about these meetings and the persons who attended these meetings. I take it from your evidence you are saying that what General Vasiljevic said is not true?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What General Vasiljevic said is not true. I did not inform General Dimitrijevic ever about meetings of some kind of Joint Command or what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you also received information about these meetings from General -- from Colonel Stefanovic, and he became head of the operations section in 1999. Did you at any time in 1999 become aware of any order issued by the corps commander purporting to emanate from the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1999, if that's what you're asking me about, so before and at all times, the corps commander issued all orders with respect to the deployment of the corps units, but in the corps command I saw several documents which had -- which were marked as -- or in the upper left-hand corner they were denoted as being the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. That's what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This was in 1999, during the war, that is, after the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- yes, after the 24th of March, thereabouts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many can you recall you saw from the corps commander after the 24th of March? Because we're interested in the -- in that period here, the war. Approximately how many. I know you can't tell us exactly. Approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three documents that I personally saw with something like that on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in all of this period of time you never, out of personal curiosity or in the position of chief of security for the corps, inquired what this purported Joint Command was about? You never satisfied yourself as to what this body was that you were writing reports addressed to; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no need for that. I don't know for what reasons I would look into that. I knew the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to ask you something. No, don't be afraid. I'm not going to say what you think I'm going to say. When Mr. Stamp asked the question, he just now said he was asking him about 1999. Now I'd like to ask you to ask him to be very precise on what he means or what year he's asking about, because it's difficult for me to follow, jumping from one to the other. I'm not going to say another word, just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me add, my colleague Mr. Fila was on his feet before me, but the question was about documents dated 1999, and then in his question he returned, Mr. Stamp returned, to meetings in 1998. So we're not clear whether he's asking about the 1999 documents or is he asking about the 1998 meetings. It's quite unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I disagree with that. I think the position's absolutely clear. The witness has been giving evidence about the situation during the war. We've had a lot of evidence already about the situation in 1998, and Mr. Stamp has clearly asked a question that relates to both periods and is asking whether the witness ever inquired what this purported Joint Command was about. So that question may be answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I don't think I was clear enough. He spoke about -- he said the report where it said "Joint Command." That's what Mr. Stamp said, and that's the article, and we're dealing with 1998. That's the point. I understood just what you understood, that he moved on to 1999; but it says the report you tabled to the Joint Command. That's the article and the article is 1998. That's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It must be some interpretation difficulty because the position's absolutely clear in English that in referring to the reports Mr. Stamp was simply using that as a description of this body, the Joint Command, whether it be 1998, when the reports were involved; or 1999, when the witness says he had seen documents that relate to the Joint Command. It's a question that covers the whole period and asks the witness to say whether throughout 1998 and 1999, don't let's be side-tracked by detailed, at any stage he asked what this body, the Joint Command, was about. Now, would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this body that the Prosecutor refers to as Joint Command, to the best of my knowledge and understanding, overall understanding from 1998, what this was about was - and I said this last time - an explanation from Colonel Djakovic, quite simply they were meetings between representatives of the army and the Ministry of the Interior at which they would, after having received orders down their own chains of command to rout and destroy the terrorist groups, would sit down and coordinate and organize joint activities to perform an action on the ground. That's how I understand the term the Prosecutor is referring to as Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question was more precise than that, and if Mr. Stamp wishes to follow it up he may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the question as put by the Court is pretty clear. In 1998 and 1999, having regard to all you heard about this so-called Joint Command that you addressed reports to and that in 1999 the corps commander -- you saw reports that the corps commander addressed reports to, did you ever inquire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, before we get bogged down. Why do you need to complicate it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever inquire as to what this so-called Joint Command was all throughout 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'll be crystal clear. During 1998 from July onwards, when I heard about this term at the beginning of July and right up to the first half of November while this term was being bandied about, I received information when I asked about it, it's the information that I've already given you. Later on in 1999, I did not hear of this term being used, nor was it used in the corps command, except for the fact that I saw two or three documents which had this heading. So to the best of my knowledge, in 1999 this coordination no longer existed except that a commander would go perhaps to the chief of SUP on occasion over some specific issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this coordination no longer existed in 1999, yet you saw after March 1999 documents issued by the corps commander with Joint Command in the top left-hand corner, indicating where they were emanating from. When you saw that, did you not inquire what this Joint Command was all about, having regard to what you understood, that it no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor coordination and cooperation between the MUP and the army was continuous throughout, and it was both the duty in 1998 and 1999 and it evolved in 19 -- it took place, existed in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking about the expression "Joint Command." When you saw that in 1999 on documents issued by your corps commander, did you not inquire what he was referring to in those documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no need. It was clear to me. I knew that just as in 1998 it referred to, it was a message to the subordinate units, and it had been dovetailed -- dovetailed cooperation and coordination between the MUP and the army so there was no need for me to ask the same thing several times over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the English version here you're recorded as saying to the best of your knowledge "in 1999 this coordination no longer existed, except that a commander would go perhaps to the chief of SUP on occasion over some specific issue." Is that an accurate record of what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, what I said is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, I want to make it clear that we would like the translation of that to be considered and the written version provided for us, that's the paragraph at page 80, the beginning of page 80. Now, what do you now want to say on that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say, Mr. President, is this, that many questions asked by the Prosecutor are, as far as I'm concerned, not understandable enough and imprecise. I wanted to give a precise answer, and that is that cooperation and coordination existed in 1999 and in 1998 as well, but that during 1999 except for seeing on a few documents in the Pristina Corps this term "Joint Command," I no longer had information and data as to whether these meetings were being held on the subject of coordination and cooperation. But I do know that cooperation and coordination still existed between the MUP and the army because it was a state of war, when I was on the ground frequently and when conditions were not the same as they had been in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem that that creates is that it would appear that in 1999 the use of the expression in your mind meant something different from 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. President. For me what this always meant is that there was coordination and cooperation between the MUP and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I may move on, having regard to the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke about disciplining of commanders. Can you tell us whether or not -- or can you tell us how many commanders were prosecuted for serious offences committed against Kosovar Albanians alleged to have been committed between 24 March to 10 June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What level of command are you referring to, brigade commanders or the commanders at any level?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I was referring to the -- to commanders at any level. Let's start there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No disciplinary measures were taken in relation to any brigade commander for any violations of the international humanitarian law, international law of war during the clashes. There was no information indicated that anything like that had occurred, but disciplinary measures were taken and charges were pressed for all sorts of other omissions that happened across the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This case is about offences that were committed against Kosovar Albanians. Can you say how many commanders were prosecuted for offences committed against -- for serious offences committed against Kosovar Albanians between 24 March and 10 June 1999? I hope you understand the question. I'm not asking you to tell us about prosecutions in general or prosecution of brigade commanders only. I'm asking you about any commander, but I restrict the question to offences committed against Kosovar Albanian, Albanian, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No commander at any command level in the corps was ever prosecuted for murder, whereas you say violations of international law of war and international rules of war; but at corps level any officer who committed a crime was prosecuted and measures were taken against those persons. If measures were taken in relation to a commander, that would have meant that his organizational unit, the unit over which he exercised command, the company, battalion, brigade, or platoon had collectively been involved in the commission of crimes. The last time when I gave evidence, I told you that these were individual incidents, individual violations, of the international humanitarian law, international law of war, and all those that we were aware of were criminally prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many involved victims -- I'll just go back to the question I asked you. How many persons that exercised command functions in the Pristina Corps were prosecuted for offences committed against Kosovar Albanians? Can you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about individual crimes? Measures were taken in relation to perpetrators, unit commanders, except, for example, unauthorised departure from the duty post, those persons were court-martialed. Some other measures were taken, but what you are implying, criminal measures, none were taken except those that were taken against perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm trying to ask you is not about crimes in general. I'm asking you about crimes committed against Kosovar Albanians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I think you need to distinguish between commanders who are prosecuted on the basis of command responsibility, which is what I think the witness thinks you're asking him, and commanders who are prosecuted because of the perpetration themselves directly of crimes. And what he's saying is no one was prosecuted as a commander at all. The only people prosecuted were prosecuted because they were perpetrators. Now, if that's wrong, he'll tell us now, if that's a wrong understanding of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are entirely right, Mr. President. As for those we actually prosecuted for crimes, they were among those platoon commanders and company commanders who were involved in crimes such as murder and the like. As I was testifying before this Trial Chamber, I did share certain information about certain specific officers, their ranks and their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. How many of these commanders that you just spoke of were prosecuted for crimes committed against Kosovar Albanians, whether it was by virtue of command responsibility or as perpetrators? Just how many do you know were prosecuted for crimes against Kosovar Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you're asking me to remember everything. Well I'll do my best, but I think you need to go back to the archives of appropriate military courts because they contain documentation in relation to every single crime, the function that those people performed and which specific officers you're looking at. I've told you this several times but I'm going to tell you again. There is a security organ that was criminally prosecuted, a major, because he had ordered two soldiers to kill two Albanian civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't want to go over ground that I've covered. I just asked you for a figure, an approximate figure, a number. How many approximately? You can tell us if you know; or if you don't know, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, based on all the surveys, I think there must have been around ten such officers, and I am talking about officers now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these were charged for offences committed against Kosovar Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was because of them that actions were instituted over crimes that they had either ordered or had been responsible for the commission of, and the crimes were perpetrated by their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- you indicate in a variety of the exhibits that we have before this Court that you were receiving information from various sources, some of them outside of Serbia, Europe, Switzerland, et cetera. So I take it that you must have become aware of the indictment in this case which was published on the 24th of May, 1999. Did you become aware of it and when?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, again you're putting to me something that I never said. I never said that I had received information from various sources from outside the country or whatever your figure of speech happened to be. I said that I obtained information by using the prescribed methodology of any military service, including the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I was referring to many of the documents that were tendered while you were testifying, many of them referred to information that you received from overseas. But be that as it may, when, if you did -- the question is this: Did you become aware of the indictment in this case for these crimes committed in Kosovo and when?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I became aware, as any other citizen of my country. I was no longer a member of the security service at the time. Between 1999 and 2003 I was not a member of the State Security Service. I did learn that an indictment was raised in this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you become aware? Is your evidence that you did not become aware of this indictment in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a little later, a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you become aware of this indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps Mr. Stamp could himself be a little more precise, since I don't think it is the same indictment -- well, in part at least -- well, I'm not suggesting anything, but more precise, yes, there. I can't speak more openly in front of the witness, but I think you know what I have in mind. The question is: Is this the same indictment we're looking at today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's so frustrating the length of time it takes to ask one simple question. Mr. Stamp, the question you want to ask is: When did the witness become aware of the indictment against, and you'll need to specify whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you become aware of an indictment issued by this Tribunal for crimes allegedly committed by Serbian security forces in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at one point it was published, the fact that the indictment had been raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah, but when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, that indictment included among its number Slobodan Milosevic. When did you first learn of an indictment in relation to him for offences committed by Serb forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, well I think that this was as early as 19 -- I really can't remember. I'm afraid I might get it wrong, but I think 1997, possibly 1996. I may be off the mark, it's a distinct possibility. Perhaps it might have been 1999 -- well, if you want me to remember as best as I can, but I don't think I can answer this question with a greater degree of accuracy than I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we're dealing with crimes which allegedly were committed in 1999 and with an anti-terrorist operation in 1998, and we're confining our attention to Kosovo. So bearing in mind when these events took place and having been told already by Mr. Stamp that the indictment was issued on the 24th of May I think, is it, 1999, when did you first learn of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just after the indictment was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's taken about ten minutes, right, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you or your service or anyone in your service in the Pristina Corps investigate any of the allegations of crimes mentioned in that indictment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, or rather, Mr. Prosecutor, we were responsible members of the security service, very much so in fact, and I know very well that we immediately documented and prosecuted all crimes committed by members of the army, with the exception of individual crimes in relation to which it was impossible to establish because of the fact that the time was short. I'm talking about three months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, that's not the question. The question is: Having seen this indictment, did you go off and investigate the allegations in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not investigate that because there was no reason for me to investigate that and I was not a member of the service after the indictment had been raised between 1999 and 2003. I had no authority to launch any investigation or take any measures that authorised members of the security service were supposed to be taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you leave your position as chief of the security department in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In August 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stamp's asking you what you did between May, when you learned about the indictment, and August 1999. Did you investigate the allegations set out in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Mr. President, checking, collecting intelligence is one of the methods used by the security organ. We never stopped gathering this sort of thing and we certainly were not indifferent, and all the indications that we had at the time after all our checks was that to a large extent, as General Geza had said, I would say to an even larger extent was we were successful in documenting and investigating all the crimes committed by members of the army, with the exception of several crimes which we investigated and we started proceedings, but it was impossible to ascertain with full certainty that these crimes had been committed by members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With respect, you have not unequivocally answered the question that the President asked you. Did you between May, when you learned of the indictment, and August 1999 investigate any of the allegations of crimes that were contained in that indictment? You have already told us you did not in respect to the Meja incident. I wish you just to answer: Yes, you did investigate; or no, you did not. Did you in that period, May to August 1999, investigate any of the crimes alleged in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not launch an investigation, there was no reason for anything like that. I know with great certainty, and I knew exactly what I did, and I knew exactly what my subordinates did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I make an inquiry of, I'm referring to the Court, having regard to the time he used, I don't think I'm up to that yet and there are a few questions more, not much, I would like to ask of the witness; however they are not the most important questions I want to ask. So if there is a need, because I understood there might be a need for him to leave today or tomorrow, then I would stop, but if there was no problem in him returning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought it was Mr. Dikovic the problem related to and that's why we interposed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, can you tell us. Is there any particular reason why Mr. Stojanovic has to run away -- sorry, rush away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were told by the VWS that they had his flight booked and he probably should be on his way. I didn't myself speak to General Stojanovic during his time under oath, but that's what we were told from the VWS, that he should be on a flight tomorrow and perhaps we should just ask him, but that's what we were told by the appropriate section.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The flight today I understand was late -- I mean, it is -- it's in the evening, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't know. Colonel Dikovic was not flying Yugoslav airlines, he was flying Lufthansa this afternoon, there were no JAT flights, but I believe the VWS people said they booked General Stojanovic on a flight tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In one sense, Mr. Stamp, your question is immaterial because it is finishing time tonight unless you were going to rush something in if the pressure was on. Is that what you were going to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If because it is my misunderstanding, I thought there might have been a problem with this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds like there is, the VWS have arrangements for travel tomorrow, and we are sitting in the afternoon and we don't know the time of that travel. That can all be checked when we rise, but just in case there is a problem is there anything particular you wanted to ask? Because you are still well within your time, but this evening we don't have time to sit on. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Respectfully, I ask that the break be taken now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If the break could be taken now and return to this witness tomorrow. The misunderstanding is this: I thought that the witness had a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- It appears the witness does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I know the Victims and Witnesses Unit makes arrangements that their return is flexible, so if that is the only issue there is flexibility in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We shall adjourn now until tomorrow. Mr. Stojanovic, I'm afraid you've got a little further to go before you're finished, and we'll need to return here to complete your evidence tomorrow. That will be at 2.15 again in this courtroom. So would you please now leave the court with the usher and return here ready to resume your evidence at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of December, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
